notes.accuracy: Protocol details check out against NIP-57 and NIP-47: lud16 to the LNURL-pay well-known path, allowsNostr and nostrPubkey, kind 9734 never published to relays, description hash as SHA-256 of the request, kind 9735 published by the wallet with p, P and e tags, and the three receipt checks. entries.title: Fine-Tuning

notes.accuracy: The arithmetic holds: 4096 squared is 16.8 million, rank 8 stores 2x4096x8 = 65,536 numbers (0.4%), and rank 4 on a 16x16 matrix holds half of 256. The preview's rank-1 panel reads 'missed 41.3%' with 'stored 32 numbers vs 256', matching the narration. The digest lists sources as empty, so the 'real' runs are not traceable to any cited source.
notes.depth: Each chapter gives a mechanism with a number: rank error curve, temperature-softened dark knowledge, int8 versus int4 error spread, the single-outlier trap and block-wise quantization, and replay holding task A at 0.01. These are introductory, though, with few trade-offs beyond the closing toolkit line.
notes.clarity: Chapter 1 defines B and A before using them. Chapter 2 says 'logits' and 'softmax' without defining them, and the narration relies on temperature alone to carry the idea. Otherwise the beats are short and speakable.
notes.story: A four-part arc in which each chapter sets up the next: a low-rank update, then a compact student, then a compressed number format, then the forgetting that compression and adaptation risk. The closing line 'every fine-tune is a negotiation with what the model already knows' ties the four together, and the low-rank nudge from chapter 1 returns in the closing toolkit.
notes.visual: The chapter 1 matrix panels and rank bars explain the idea well, but the bottom bar chart is cropped at the frame edge and crowded by the caption. The chapter 2 teacher and student bars are clean and legible. In chapter 4 the title and the 'task A lives here' labels are overdrawn by the curve and low in contrast, and the strip chart has no y-axis label.
notes.sync: Cue counts match captions in all four chapters. Tails are 11.3 to 14.9 seconds, with chapter 4 at the 15-second edge. Pacing in chapter 2 is uneven, dropping to 129 wpm at one cue and then 190 wpm at the next. I cannot see the motion, so this is timing-only and I cap it at the honest range.
notes.sound: Average pace is 162 to 171 wpm, within the good range. Acronyms are spelled out ('low rank adaptation', 'eight bits'), which avoids pronunciation risk. Some cues reach 186 to 190 wpm. Audio is 1.5 to 1.7 MB for 94 to 109 seconds, which is sensible. I inferred this from the digest; I did not hear it.

issues.problem: The digest lists sources as empty. The reported 'real' SVD, distillation and replay runs have no cited source or reproduction reference.

entries.bestMoment: The chapter 1 reveal: a 16x16 update where the rank-one reconstruction misses 41% of the matrix, which is the first concrete sign that the change lives in a thin slice of weight space.

entries.title: Evaluation

notes.accuracy: Concrete figures (train error 4e-18, fresh error 3.74, calibration gap 24 to 4 points) are presented as measured, but the digest lists sources as empty, so nothing is cited, and Goodhart's law and the contamination story go uncited. Chapter 4 says 47% of paired runs reverse and chapter 5 says 48%, with different run counts and no reconciliation.
notes.depth: Mechanisms are real: memorization versus generalization, the reliability diagram, temperature scaling, the square-root-of-n noise argument. Edge cases and trade-offs (cost of temperature scaling, when fresh test sets are impractical) are thin, so it stays at survey-plus-numbers depth.
notes.clarity: Each chapter defines its one idea before using it (the reliability diagram is introduced as a lie detector before any bars appear). Sentences are short and speakable. Some beats lean on rhetorical contrast more than explanation.
notes.story: Strong arc: a hook about memorizing homework, then build through Goodhart, calibration and variance, then a payoff in a gauntlet that reuses the memorizer and the plus-one claim. The chapter 4 question 'better, or lucky?' is paid off in chapter 5, and the closing line 'the honest evaluation is the one that wants to catch you' is memorable.
notes.visual: The chapter 1 memorizer curve carries the idea well, but its label collides with the curve's left spike and the curve is clipped at the frame edges. entries.title: The Query Cache

notes.accuracy: The numbers check out: 10B queries/month is about 3,900 requests/s (roughly the stated 4,000), and 10B x 270 bytes is 2.7 TB, matching the narration's 'nearly three terabytes'. The LRU mechanics (hash table plus doubly linked list, promote on hit, evict tail on set) match the scene header. The sources list is empty, though the header names the README and snippets.
notes.depth: Good use of concrete numbers (250 microseconds per megabyte from memory, SSD 4x, disk 80x) and a real trade-off between per-machine caches, full copies and sharding. It skips consistent hashing, which the header cites, and says nothing about rebalancing when machines join or leave, or about stampedes when a hot entry expires.
notes.clarity: Each beat introduces one idea, and terms such as cache aside, TTL and hash table are defined in plain words. 'Query A P I' is spelled out for speech. The chapter 2 mechanics are easy to follow with the car-chain metaphor.
notes.story: Problem (4,000 requests a second), machine (LRU), then the stale and sharded payoff makes a tidy build. Chapter 1's question ('what to keep, what to evict, when to stop trusting an answer') is paid off in chapters 2 and 3. The final cue is a recap list ('Parse... Serve... Expire... Shard'), which lands as a summary rather than a closing image.
notes.visual: Chapter 1's mid-chapter frame is faded, with the header stats nearly invisible against the background. Chapter 2 is clean, with the hash table and linked list legible and the tail highlighted. Chapter 3 keeps the Memory Cache panel central, though the TTL clocks are tiny.
notes.sync: Caption and cue counts match in all three chapters. Chapter 3's last cue starts 16.0s before the chapter ends, which is past the 15s tail threshold and may leave dead air at the end. Other cues run at 143-200 wpm, and the tails of chapters 1 and 2 are normal.
notes.sound: Overall pacing of 166-175 wpm is in the good band, with the opening at 200 wpm, which is quick but acceptable. Spelled-out acronyms are handled deliberately. Audio files of about 1.5 to 1.7 MB for 99 to 108 seconds are sensible. I inferred this from the digest; I could not hear the narration.

issues.problem: The last narration cue starts 16.0s before the chapter ends, a tail longer than the ~15s threshold, which risks dead air over the closing visual.

issues.problem: Sharding is presented as hash(query) mod machines with no mention of what happens when machines are added or removed, even though the header cites consistent hashing.

notes.accuracy: Backprop arithmetic checks out and matches the on-screen labels: loss 0.5×0.2² = 0.02, ∂L/∂ŷ = 0.20, ∂L/∂w2 = 0.20, and ∂L/∂z1 = 0.24, so the first-weight gradient is 0.24×1.5 = 0.36. The optimizer behaviour described is standard. The digest lists sources as empty, and the book cites no external reference, so grounding rests on the scene files. The diffusion line 'learns… which direction is less noisy' is a loose gloss of the score function, which points toward higher density.
notes.depth: Backprop is the deepest chapter: real numbers, a chain-rule walkthrough and a convergence trace. Attention omits the 1/√d scaling and multi-head structure. Diffusion has no noise schedule or training objective, and gradient descent stays at a qualitative level.
notes.clarity: Narration is written for the ear: short sentences, 'point zero two' spelled out, and Q/K/V defined before use. Forward and Backward are labelled as beats. Terms such as 'embedding space' and 'differentiable lookup table' get a plain gloss.
notes.story: Four largely independent topics. Ch1 says 'the shape of the loss decides the race' and never returns to it. Ch2 ends 'That's training', and ch3 is a detour. Only ch4's 'Sampling is denoising' gives a closing thought, and nothing carries a planted question through to a payoff.
notes.visual: Ch1 is strong: the landscape and the three trajectories carry the idea. Ch4's noise-field arrows show the idea well. Ch2 has an overprint: the '∂L/∂ŷ = ŷ − y = 0.20' label runs under the 'L = ½(ŷ−y)² = 0.020' formula in the top right, which hurts legibility. The ch4 frame at high timestep does not show the two moons, which weakens the link to the blurb.
notes.sync: Caption counts match cue counts in all four chapters, and the cues are evenly spaced at about 10s in ch4. Tails are 4.9–8.5s, inside the limit. Ch3's 'Every token does this at once' runs at about 210 wpm for 4.8s. I cannot see motion, so this stays in the 6.5 band.
notes.sound: Rates are 147–169 wpm overall, a good band. Only ch3's final fast caption goes above 200. Symbols are spoken as words, and the audio size (about 15 KB/s) is sensible. Inferred, not heard.
notes.curiosity: 'Two moons appear that never existed anywhere' and 'a soft, differentiable lookup table' are memorable hooks. The book offers no next step, though, and the chapters do not open new questions for one another.

entries.title: Neural Networks

notes.accuracy: The perceptron update (w += y x, b += y), the ReLU hinge, the sin-based loss surface and the 1958 attribution all match the scene header and the on-screen formulas; the sin(b x) symmetry claim in ch3 holds. Unverifiable specifics such as 'eighteen of thirty-two points' and 'eight updates over four passes' are asserted without a visible counter, and the sources list is empty.
notes.depth: Covers real mechanisms (convergence guarantee, saddles vs local minima, train vs test U-curve, ridge penalty) but stays at the level of intuition, with few numbers, edge cases or trade-offs beyond 'depth needs bends'. An expert would find the ch3 and ch5 treatments thin.
notes.clarity: Terms such as weights, bias, hinge, loss and lambda are introduced before use, and sentences are short and speakable. Beats are one idea each. Some cues stack two claims, as in the ch5 'dropout in spirit' line.
notes.story: Clear arc: ch1 hits a wall (no straight line works), ch2 bends it, ch3 finds the terrain problem, ch4 shows overfitting, ch5 pays off with regularization. The ch1 planted question ('what happens when no straight line can do the job') is paid in ch2 and the chapters connect. The closing line 'buy accuracy on the data you have never seen' is memorable.
notes.visual: The ch1 perceptron frame is clean and legible, with the separating line, weight arrow and formula carrying the idea. The ch3 frame shows the 'a shallow local minimum' label colliding with a faded 'frequency' label, plus ghosted leftover panel text behind the contour plot. entries.title: Recordings Become Practice

entries.title: Training

notes.accuracy: Specifics are grounded: the eta < 2/lambda stability limit (the ch1 frame shows 'safe only below 0.08' for lambda 25), momentum reducing the gap to sqrt(kappa), and the 1/sqrt(B) batch-noise rate all match standard results. notes.depth: Each chapter gives a concrete mechanism and a measured number: 25x condition number, 97 vs 1 steps, 0.06 vs 0.01 vs under 0.005 final loss, a 1/sqrt(B) spread over 400 batches, and a bias-variance split checked to the third decimal. notes.clarity: Each beat is short and the terms are mostly defined when used. 'Eigenvalues' appears in ch1 with no gloss, which a newcomer will stumble on, and the bias-variance chapter introduces two new habits of error at once.
notes.story: The arc runs from a stretched valley to schedules to batch size to error decomposition, with a recap in the closing lines. The bias-variance chapter sits a bit apart from the optimization thread, and the book's question of how to shape steps is only partly carried into it.
notes.visual: Ch1 two-panel bowl and safe-range bars are clean and readable. Ch3 has the legend (batch 1/8/64) overlapping the L(w,c) formula. Ch4 has deg-9 curves clipping at a hard horizontal edge near the top right.

entries.title: State-Space Models

notes.accuracy: The scene header names real computations (N=6 SSM, 48 steps, copy task at recall 0.05 vs 1.00, 6.7e-16 duality diff, 512 KiB KV per token vs 64 MiB state, 0.65/0.65 and 1.00/-0.16 delta-rule reads) and the memory arithmetic checks out (2 GiB at 4k, 64 GiB at 128k, 1024x). notes.curiosity: The 'identity earns a route' framing is an appealing mental model, and 'proof, not a name' is a memorable idea. The book does not end on an open question or a 'try this' hook, so it satisfies more than it provokes.

issues.problem: 'Biscuit' is introduced as a token ('A Biscuit token now binds the peer...') with no gloss, and 'protobuf' and 'enrollment request' also arrive unexplained.
issues.fix: Add a one-clause definition the first time Biscuit appears (for example, 'a signed, attenuable token that carries the peer's roles'), and gloss protobuf in a few words.

issues.problem: The closing beat is a four-item recap ('identity, route, discovery, and a tool call') rather than a payoff, and no question planted earlier is answered.
issues.fix: Plant a question in chapter 1 (for example, 'what happens when the proof is missing?') and answer it in the closing line.

issues.problem: The final cue ('Router addresses come back with the proof...') runs at about 243 wpm for roughly 4 seconds, which will sound crammed.
issues.fix: Split the line into two captions or trim it so it lands under 180 wpm.

issues.problem: Depth is thin: there are no numbers, token lifetimes, role counts, or failure modes beyond 'an unknown caller stops at the gate'.
issues.fix: Add one concrete figure or edge case per chapter (for example, what a rejected Biscuit does, or how many roles a peer can carry).

issues.problem: The chapter 2 frame is sparse: the 'VerifyBiscuit' and 'trusted public keys' labels float without connectors, and the Biscuit label overlaps the icon.
issues.fix: Draw the arrows from the trusted keys to the gate and enlarge the Biscuit label.

entries.bestMoment: 'A node starts with one local secret, and nothing in the mesh can trust it yet' gives a clear, concrete hook, and the chapter 1 frame shows the enrollment flow cleanly.

entries.title: The Side Table
entries.subtitle: Six shop techniques, one kitchen side table

notes.accuracy: Specific, source-grounded details (sixteen pieces, 1x8 and 2x4 lumber, the cabinetmaker's triangle quote, cauls, scrap pads, chisel-off squeeze-out, steaming dents before 220 grit) match the scene headers. Overclaim in ch2: 'a properly fitted edge joint is stronger than the wood on either side' is stated as fact with no hedge. The digest also lists sources as empty even though the headers cite Lee Valley.
notes.depth: Mechanisms are real: why cauls stop buckling without adding squeeze, why end grain is routed first so side passes remove tear-out, and why sanding before steaming levels the dent. Trade-offs are thin, though; the book rarely says what a reader would give up by doing it the other way.
notes.clarity: Terms are introduced before use and sentences are short enough to speak. 'Cauls' is defined in context ('stiff bars clamped across the panel'). Ch2 gets dense in its second half, where several beats stack up.
notes.story: The triangle planted in ch1 pays off in the 'one of them goes back turned around' beat, and the closing line 'decide the order before you start' ties the four builds together. The arc is hook, build, payoff, and the chapters connect.
notes.visual: The preview frames are clean and legible. The ch1 triangle over four boards carries the idea well, and the ch2 end-on panel with cauls and pads is clear. The ch4 caption box overlaps the bottom edge of the routed panel, and the ch1 side-table sketch on the right is too small to read.
notes.sync: Caption and cue counts match in all four chapters, and the last cue sits 4.5 to 11.7 s before each chapter ends, which is normal. Ch2 bursts to 248-262 wpm on its last captions, so beats there feel crammed. I could not judge the motion itself, so this stays in the middle range.
notes.sound: Overall pace is 191 to 216 wpm, above the 110-170 target and past the 185 'rushed' line in every chapter. Ch2 is the worst at 216 wpm. Audio runs about 125 kbps, which is sensible for the duration. Pronunciation risks are low; 'cabinetmaker's' and '1x8' are the only ones I noticed.
notes.curiosity: The triangle trick and the router-order trick give a reader two portable mental models. The book does not leave a sharp open question at the end, and there is no next-episode hook beyond the series label.

issues.problem: Narration runs 248-262 wpm in the back half of the chapter, and the overall rate is 216 wpm.
issues.fix: Split the long sentences in the 'Squeeze the joints' and 'What comes out of the clamps' beats, or cut about 15% of the words so the chapter sits near 170-185 wpm.

issues.problem: 'A properly fitted edge joint is stronger than the wood on either side of it' is an uncited, unhedged claim.
issues.fix: Soften it ('a well-fitted edge joint can be as strong as the surrounding wood') or cite the source that supports it.

issues.problem: The digest lists sources as empty, but the scene headers cite Lee Valley's article, so the book's provenance is not recorded in its metadata.
issues.fix: Add the Lee Valley article and author to the book's sources field so the grounding is visible to viewers and graders.

issues.problem: The caption box overlaps the bottom edge of the routed panel in the ch4 preview frame.
issues.fix: Move the panel up or reduce its size so the caption sits in clear space below it.

issues.problem: The side-table sketch on the right of the ch1 frame is tiny, and its labels are hard to read.
issues.fix: Enlarge the sketch or drop it from the frame and let the triangle carry the picture.

entries.bestMoment: Ch1's 'Turn that board back and the lines meet again. You checked an assembly in about a second, without measuring anything at all' turns the planted triangle into a concrete payoff.

entries.title: A Week With Replay QA
entries.subtitle: What it means for you, from Monday to ship day

notes.accuracy: Chapter 1's header says the field, walks and HUD counts are seeded synthetic data, but the narration presents 'an agent opens your app in a real browser' as fact, and the book's sources list is empty. Claims are mostly product-level and not tied to a named mechanism.
notes.depth: Mostly an overview of the workflow: Monday paste, Tuesday tape, Wednesday fix, Thursday PR check, month-later coverage. There are no numbers beyond the synthetic counts, no edge cases, and no trade-offs. An expert would learn little that is new.
notes.clarity: Short, speakable sentences, and each chapter has one idea ('bad news arrives carrying its own proof'). The terms 'moment', 'trail' and 'field' are introduced visually in chapter 1 and then reused consistently.
notes.story: The week gives a clear arc: setup, a bug with proof, a fix that must be checked, a PR, and a payoff in 'You didn't hire a tester. You hired a witness.' The question 'is it really fixed?' from chapter 3 is paid off by the green check, and the chapters connect rather than list.
notes.visual: Previews are clean and legible. Chapter 1 is sparse, with a small agent dot and a readable caption. Chapter 3's tape comparison carries the idea well, but the bug card is clipped at the top edge of the frame. Chapter 5's coverage field is attractive but dense.
notes.sync: Caption and cue counts match in all five chapters. The last cue sits 1.5 to 4.5 seconds before each chapter end, which is normal. Ch1 has a 251 wpm cue at 17.4s and a 245 wpm cue at 27.3s, so the pacing is uneven in that chapter. I could not judge the motion itself.
notes.sound: Pacing is mostly 170 to 230 wpm and sometimes above the 185 wpm rushed mark, which is a risk for a narrated book. Chapter 5 is slower at 180 wpm overall, which is fine. There are no acronyms or code identifiers in the narration, so pronunciation risk is low. Audio sizes are sensible for their durations. I inferred these from the text, not by listening.
notes.curiosity: The core model, 'a witness is cheap, a tape is the currency', is sharp. The book is more reassuring than provocative, though, and it leaves little that makes a reader want to try it or dig into how the agent works.

issues.problem: The synthetic-data disclaimer appears only in the scene comment, while the narration states 'an agent opens your app in a real browser' and 'every dot is a moment someone could visit' as plain fact. The book's sources list is empty.
issues.fix: Add an on-screen or spoken note that the field is illustrative, and list the grounding sources in the book metadata.

issues.problem: Depth stays at the level of a product overview. Nothing explains how a 'moment' is defined, how a trail is recorded, or what gets re-walked, so an expert gets no mechanism.
issues.fix: Add one beat that names a concrete mechanism, such as what counts as a moment, or what a re-walk actually replays.

issues.problem: Narration runs at 251 wpm at 17.4s and 245 wpm at 27.3s, which squeezes two beats into short gaps.
issues.fix: Split the long sentences or move one beat so that no cue exceeds about 200 wpm.

issues.problem: In the preview frame the bug card is clipped at the top edge of the frame, which reads as a layout error.
issues.fix: Shift the bug card and the tape group down so the card has a full margin.

issues.problem: The closing beats are strong, but the coverage field and the calendar strip compete for attention in the same frame.
issues.fix: Fade the calendar strip out before the field lights up, so each frame has one focus.

entries.bestMoment: 'You didn't hire a tester. You hired a witness.'

entries.title: Tab Into the Future
entries.subtitle: A browser that meets you halfway

notes.accuracy: Claims are carefully hedged ("proposed", "not claimed passed", "opt-in"), and the scene headers cite a pinned charter and W3C focus-order guidance. But the book's sources array is empty, so the grounding cannot be checked from the digest.
notes.depth: Mechanisms are present (suggestion vs. focus vs. activation, Escape/reverse-Tab compatibility, shadow mode, versioned feedback buffer), but there are no numbers, thresholds, or worked edge cases. Ch2 names the echo problem without showing how the label schema would separate evidence.
notes.clarity: Plain, speakable sentences with one idea per beat. The focus ring vs. suggestion distinction is set up clearly in Ch1 and reused well.
notes.story: Clear arc from the Tab-accept hook ("bring the machinery back to the person") through the echo problem in Ch2 to the pilot path in Ch3. The closing line ("a quiet suggestion and a press of Tab") pays off the opening. The stakes are somewhat abstract.
notes.visual: Ch1 is a clean, legible composition in which the page, the dashed suggestion, and the solid focus ring are visibly distinct. Ch2's timeline carries the idea well. Ch3 has collisions: the dashed suggestion box overlaps the 'Display name' label, the 'narrow baseline' label is clipped at the card edge, and the pill row runs to the right edge.
notes.sync: Eight captions match eight cues in each chapter. The last cue sits 7-9s before the chapter end, which is a normal tail. Pacing is even within chapters. I could not see the motion, so this is a timing-only judgment.
notes.sound: Overall 175 wpm in Ch1 is at the rushed edge, and the 208 and 206 wpm opening and closing cues go past the 185 wpm threshold. Ch2-3 sit at 155-156 wpm, which is comfortable. Audio is 1.1-1.2 MB for 69-77s, which is sensible. I inferred the rest.
notes.curiosity: The 'learning from its own echo' question is a sharp mental model that will stick. The book does not, however, invite the viewer to try anything or go further than the proposal.

issues.problem: The book's sources array is empty even though scene headers cite pinned charter sections and W3C guidance, so the grounding claims are not visible in the metadata.
issues.fix: Populate sources with the charter and W3C references the scene headers name, or add a footnote linking each chapter's claims to them.

issues.problem: Narration pacing runs fast: the opening caption is 208 wpm, the caption at 53.7s is 185 wpm, and the closing caption is about 206 wpm. Overall Ch1 is 175 wpm.
issues.fix: Split the long opening and closing sentences, or add a half-beat pause before the closing line so it lands rather than rushes.

issues.problem: Label collisions in the preview: the dashed suggestion box overlaps the 'Display name' label, the 'narrow baseline' label is clipped at the card edge, and the bottom pill row runs close to the right edge.
issues.fix: Offset the suggestion outline below the label, move the timeline labels inside the card bounds, and narrow the pill row or wrap it.

issues.problem: Depth stays at the level of the claim. The evidence labels (goal, source, outcome) are named but never shown in a concrete example, such as one logged Tab acceptance followed by a dismissal.
issues.fix: Add one worked example of a feedback record and how it is labelled, to make the echo problem concrete.

issues.problem: Pacing is uneven: the caption at 27.9s runs 129 wpm, while the closing caption at 68.2s runs 193 wpm, so the final beat is the fastest in the chapter.
issues.fix: Even out the caption lengths in Ch3 so the closing line is not rushed.

entries.bestMoment: "The experience we want is simple: the browser offers the next useful place, and the person remains the one who chooses to go there."

entries.title: How to Build a Shed
entries.subtitle: An 8-foot cube, from level ground to raising day

notes.accuracy: Procedural claims (8-ft boards, 4x8 sheets, 16-in joist spacing, 7/16 OSB, 22.5-degree trusses) match the scene header's cited Instructables guide. But the digest lists sources as empty, and the chapter 1 'needs no permit at all' line overgeneralizes a rule that varies by city.
notes.depth: Mostly a sequence of steps. Squareness checks, lapped rims, and the flat-framing trick give some mechanism, but there are few trade-offs or failure modes (what goes wrong with a skipped diagonal check or an unlevel pier).
notes.clarity: Plain, speakable sentences and a clear through-line. Trade names and trade terms go undefined: 'toe-screwed', 'tongue-and-groove', 'strand board', 'pressure-treated', 'counterbored'.
notes.story: Good arc. The 'twelve-inch problem' from chapter 1 is planted and paid off in chapter 2, the floor becomes 'the factory' in chapter 3, and the closing 'Go build one' lands. Chapters connect rather than list.
notes.visual: Preview ch1 (isometric cube with callouts) and ch3 (plan-view frame with hangers) are clean and legible, and the ch5 house frame carries the sheathing idea. The ch3 frame is sparse and the caption text is small.
notes.sync: Caption count matches cue count in every chapter and tails are short (6.7 to 11.3s). But several cues run above 200 wpm (ch2 232 at 85.5s, ch5 242 at 42.2s and 228 at 20.0s), so some beats are crammed. I could not see the motion, so this is timing-only.
notes.sound: Overall pacing is 166 to 185 wpm, inside the good band, with bursts above 200. Numbers are spelled out ('seven-sixteenths', 'twenty-two and a half'), which helps narration. Acronyms are minimal. I inferred this from text, not audio.
notes.curiosity: The cube-first framing and the 'one level cube on ground that has to be convinced first' hook pull the viewer in. It is mostly a how-to, though, so it leaves little open-ended question or new mental model behind.

issues.problem: Narration says a shed under 120 sq ft 'needs no permit at all' in 'the builder's city'. That overstates a rule that varies by jurisdiction and is only partly hedged by the next line.
issues.fix: Change to 'often needs no permit' and name the rule as a local check. Add a source for the code claim.

issues.problem: Several cues run far above the 110-170 wpm band (242 wpm at 42.2s, 228 wpm at 20.0s, 216 wpm at 87.6s). Those lines are crammed into short gaps, which reads as rushed.
issues.fix: Split the long lines into two captions, or give those beats more time so the pace evens out.

issues.problem: The floor section is a list of build steps with no trade-off or failure mode, which keeps depth at a how-to level.
issues.fix: Add one consequence per step, for example what a skipped diagonal check does to the door later, or why 16-in joists beat 24-in for a floor.

issues.problem: Terms like 'landscaping adhesive', 'pier block' and 'riser' appear without a plain-language gloss.
issues.fix: Add a short parenthetical on first use, such as 'a concrete block that holds the post above the ground'.

issues.problem: The digest lists 'sources: []' even though the scene headers cite a specific guide. Credits and provenance are not visible in the book's own metadata.
issues.fix: Add the Instructables guide as a source in the book metadata and an on-screen credit.

entries.bestMoment: Chapter 3's closing line, 'The floor is the factory', turns the flat platform into the workbench for the walls and trusses that follow.

entries.title: Who You Are
entries.subtitle: keys, npubs, DNS names, and follows

notes.accuracy: Specific and checkable: 256 bits regrouped into 52 five-bit words, a 6-character checksum, NIP-05 well-known/nostr.json with names and relays, and the NIP-39 proof sentence. The header says the bech32 is verified against NIP-19's test vector, which is a strong grounding claim. Nothing is overclaimed.
notes.depth: Chapters 2 to 5 carry real mechanics: bech32 cut into 5-bit words, nprofile TLV boxes, NIP-05 verification and reassignment risk, petname chains, NIP-39 proofs. Chapter 1 is mostly a list of profile fields, so the depth is uneven.
notes.clarity: The narration repeats chapter 1's intro ("On nostr, who you are is a thirty-two byte public key…" and the profile/NIP-24/replaceable lines) at the end of chapters 2, 3, 4 and 5. A newcomer hears the same five sentences four times, and the middle of the book gets lost.
notes.story: The 'coats' metaphor is a real through-line, and the closing 'On nostr, you are your key. Everything else is a coat.' lands. The repeated opening in chapters 2 to 5 undercuts the build-to-payoff arc.
notes.visual: Preview frames are clear. Chapter 3 (GET nostr.json with the names map and a matching-bytes check) is the strongest. Chapter 5 has three proof cards with checkmarks, but the dashed connectors cross the faded tag text. Chapter 1's left JSON is nearly invisible and the bottom half is empty. Judged from 3 of 5 previews only.
notes.sync: Caption count does not match cue count in chapters 2 to 5: 15, 14, 14 and 22 captions against 8, 7, 7 and 7 cues. Roughly 35 captions have no timing. Chapter 5 runs at 533 wpm across its captions and ends with a 12.5s tail. Chapter 1, the only chapter with normal timing, is fine.
notes.sound: Aggregate pacing is off: chapter 5 has 722 words in 81s, which is 533 wpm and rushed, and chapter 3 is 339 wpm. Chapter 1 (162 wpm) is good. Spelled-out pronunciations ('nip nineteen', 'bech thirty two') are sensible. Audio sizes look plausible, but I could not hear it, so the pacing finding rests on the narration text.
notes.curiosity: The 'coats' framing and 'the name is decoration' line make a reader want to try a NIP-05 or NIP-39 check. The closing claim that identity survives every claim changing is a memorable mental model.

issues.problem: Chapters 2 to 5 replay chapter 1's narration. Chapter 2 ends with seven chapter-1 captions ('On nostr, who you are…' through 'Next: how that same key learns to dress for humans'), which also appear again in chapters 3, 4 and 5.
issues.fix: Remove the chapter-1 import from the caption sources of chapters 2 to 5, so each scene carries only its own narration.

issues.problem: Chapter 5 has 22 captions against 7 narration-clock cues, so about 15 captions have no timing. It runs at 533 wpm across the chapter and ends with a 12.5s tail.
issues.fix: After removing the replayed captions, give each remaining caption its own cue and check that the chapter-5 total is near 240 words.

issues.problem: Chapter 3 has 14 captions against 7 cues. Seven are chapter-1 copies, and the chapter ends on the chapter-1 'Next:' line, so the NIP-05 payoff is buried.
issues.fix: Same caption-source fix. Give the eight chapter-3 lines their own cues.

issues.problem: The left-hand kind-0 JSON is almost invisible in the mid-chapter frame, so the 'content' string the narration unfolds is not legible. The bottom half of the canvas is empty.
issues.fix: Raise the contrast on the event fields and use the empty space, for example for the replaceable-event 'newest wins' card.

issues.problem: In the proof frame the dashed connector lines cross the faded 'i' tag text ('twitter:semisol_public'), which adds clutter to the one readable part of the event.
issues.fix: Route the connectors beneath the text layer or fade them further where they cross the tags.

entries.bestMoment: Chapter 5's closing: 'On nostr, you are your key. Everything else is a coat.'

entries.title: Electric Stream Protocol
entries.subtitle: Why the stream is the product

notes.accuracy: The digest lists no sources, and the scene header comments name no files, symbols or docs. Claims such as 'a post-clone activation hook discovers the stream identity' and 'Stream-Next-Offset' cannot be checked against anything, so the narration reads as a generic model of event streams.
notes.depth: Mechanisms stay at the level of offsets, bookmarks, quorum, and digests. The numbers (offset 42/43, quorum 4/5) are illustrative, and there are no trade-offs or edge cases beyond 'an offline client catches up' and 'a branch conflict is marked'. An expert would find it glossy.
notes.clarity: The language is plain, and the sentences are short and speakable. Terms such as projection, reducer and digest are used before they are defined, and ch4 stacks several abstractions (commit graph, working tree, object store) in one beat.
notes.story: The five chapters move from a single mutation to convergence to Git at the edge, and the reader who 'disappears' in ch1 comes back in ch3. The payoff is weaker than the setup, and the close ('the stream is authority') is a tidy summary rather than a sharp line.
notes.visual: Previews for ch1, ch3 and ch5 are clean, and the diagrams carry the flow (writer to stream to readers; quorum and offline client; clone to hook to stream to peers). Node text is small, and in ch5 the 'PROVE' badge clips the card edge and the 'digest' label sits on an arrow.
notes.sync: Cue counts match captions in every chapter, and the tails are about 10 seconds, which is normal. Several cues run at 280 to 296 wpm (ch1 at 28.8s and 43.2s, ch3 at 13.8s, ch4 at 0.5s), so some beats are crammed into short gaps. I could not see the motion itself.
notes.sound: Overall pace is 206 to 231 wpm across all five chapters, well above the 185 wpm threshold for rushed narration. Audio is about 200 to 230 KB per chapter, a sensible size for 52 to 60 seconds. This is inferred from the digest, not heard.
notes.curiosity: The 'transport is replaceable; the history is the source of truth' idea is a useful mental model, and the reader-disappears demo is a good hook. Nothing sharp is left open for the viewer to try or explore.

issues.problem: Narration runs at 280 to 290 wpm in short gaps (cues at 28.8s and 43.2s), and the overall pace is 231 wpm, which will sound rushed.
issues.fix: Cut the narration by about 20 to 25 percent or stretch the timeline so no cue exceeds about 200 wpm and the overall pace is under 185 wpm.

issues.problem: Scene header comments and the digest name no source files, and the book has no sources, so the stream mechanisms (offsets, bookmarks, activation hook) are unverifiable.
issues.fix: Ground each chapter in named files or docs in the scene header, or add sources to the digest, and tie the narration to them.

issues.problem: The quorum example (5 clients, 4/5 ready, offset 43) is illustrative but is narrated as how the system behaves, with no mechanism shown for the quorum rule.
issues.fix: Say that the example is a scenario, or show the actual quorum and commit rule from the code.

issues.problem: Ch4's opening cue runs at 296 wpm, and several beats sit at 240 to 290 wpm, so the branch concept is hard to follow.
issues.fix: Split the opening beat into two and slow the delivery so the commit-graph point lands.

issues.problem: The 'PROVE' badge clips the peer card edge, and the 'digest' label sits on an arrow line.
issues.fix: Offset the badge inside the card and move the digest label off the connector.

entries.bestMoment: Ch1 closes with 'Transport is replaceable; the durable ordered history is what gives every client, projection, and replay the same source of truth.'
